sentences.text: Nipponosaurus was a duck-billed dinosaur belonging to the lambeosaurine group, found in rock layers on Sakhalin island.
The main skeleton is about sixty percent complete, representing an immature individual roughly four meters long.
Remains include parts of the skull, neck, back, and tail, along with significant portions of the shoulder and leg bones.
This species holds the distinction of being the first dinosaur named from a fossil discovered in Japanese territory.
Despite its small size of four meters, the specimen provides a rare look at a young duck-billed dinosaur.
Takumi Nagao discovered the holotype in November 1934 while a hospital was being built for the Kawakami mine.
Additional limb bones belonging to the same animal were recovered during a second expedition in 1937.
The fossils came from the upper Yezo Group, which was once known as the upper ammonite bed.
Sediment evidence suggests the animal died and was buried in a marine environment near the shore.
This implies the species likely lived on low plains close to the coast, similar to some North American relatives.
Researchers note that the jaw bone overlaps with the teeth in a way that might indicate different feeding habits.
Originally placed in Trachodontidae, the family name is now Hadrosauridae because Trachodon is considered invalid.
A 2004 study placed it near Hypacrosaurus altispinus within the Lambeosaurinae subgroup.
Later analysis of the ischial foot size moved the species to a more basal position in Corythosaurini.
Its parent group is the Lambeosaurinae.
The creature lived during the late Cretaceous, specifically between 85.7 and 72.2 million years ago.
Associated mollusks suggest it inhabited the upper Santonian or lower Campanian stages of this time period.
The validity of Nipponosaurus is debated, with some authors calling it a nomen dubium due to its immature state and unclear features.
Recent work suggests it may be more closely related to European taxa like Arenysaurus and Blasisaurus than to North American forms.
